newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. sergeant in Germany cleared of rape.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sergeant in Germany cleared of rape.

text.p: A U.S. military jury in Germany on Thursday acquitted an army sergeant of rape and sodomy charges but found him guilty of lesser offences in the latest sex scandal to taint the American armed forces.
Sergeant First Class Julius Davis, 37, of Fayetteville, North Carolina, was found guilty on 11 of 32 counts.
The five-member all-male military panel will now decide on punishment for Davis, who Judge Gary Jewell said could face up to 32 years in prison and a dishonourable discharge.

Davis was convicted of four cases of indecent assault, four of maltreatment and one count each of fraternisation, obstruction and disobeying an order. He was found not guilty on six counts of rape, one of sodomy and other assault charges.
One of the witnesses, who told the court Davis sexually harassed her while in Bosnia, said she accepted the verdict.
"I have to accept the verdict of the jury even though I may not agree to it," Specialist Brenda Hays told Reuters.

Davis is the first soldier to be convicted outside the United States as part of the army's probe of abuse allegations at bases around the world that started after charges of rape and harassment surfaced last year at a U.S. base in Germany.

He was one of three sergeants accused of sex-related crimes at the Darmstadt base where soldiers attend an orientation programme after arriving in Germany for duty. The commander of the centre, who is a man, has been replaced by a woman.
One of the other soldiers, Sergeant First Class Paul Fuller, 26, of Columbus, Ohio, is to stand trial next week.

Defence attorneys had attacked the credibility of the 15 women soldiers who made allegations against Davis, saying there was no medical evidence to support the six counts of rape filed against him and that prosecutors launched a "witchhunt".
The U.S. armed forces have been hit by a recent series of sex scandals.
Three sergeants at the Aberdeen Proving Ground base in Maryland have been convicted on rape and harassment charges, including one who was given 25 years in jail.

Scandal has also spread to the military's Pentagon headquarters in Washington where the army's top enlisted soldier, Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney, was put on forced leave after female soldiers made harassment allegations.

Defence attorneys in Germany did not mention race as a possible motivation for the charges against Davis, as had been claimed in the Aberdeen cases. But they selected the panel of jurors on the basis of their views on inter-racial dating.
Davis is black, while most of the women who made allegations against him were white and of lower military rank, according to army officials.
